series: Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 3.1 · October 2026
title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt

slides.title: Guarantee the Contract, Not the Debt
slides.subtitle: A payment intermediary for clean power in developing countries
slides.message: Investors price the risk that a state distribution company will not pay. A payment intermediary buys power under one standard contract, pays generators in full and on time, and collects arrears behind a guarantee waterfall agreed in advance.
slides.author: Stephen J. Stretton · writing in a personal capacity

slides.title: The buyer is the risk: long arrears and poor recovery add up to 4 points to the cost of capital
slides.note: Only two of 39 Sub-Saharan African power sectors were financially viable (World Bank, 2016). Investors charge for long arrears and poor recovery, not for occasional lateness.
slides.source: Working paper 3.1, Table 2: one-year episodes, base WACC 8%, price of risk 2 (stylized); Trimble et al. (2016).

slides.title: A payment intermediary pays generators whatever the buyer does, behind a waterfall agreed in advance

points.text: The facility buys from every generator on the same power purchase agreement and sells on to distribution companies.

points.lead: Paid in full and on time.
points.text: The buyer's arrears become a debt to the facility, a repeat creditor with more leverage than any developer.
distribution company, then its state owner, the national government (intercept of transfers), a multilateral agency, a donor account.
so a crisis runs by contract, and the first calls fall on the governments that control the utility.

slides.title: The saving is real only if the facility collects better or makes default rarer

points.lead: With no price of risk and no better collection,
points.text: the guarantee only moves the expected loss from investors to the state.

points.lead: Better collection is a real gain:
points.text: at 80% recovery the saving rises from $2.0 to $3.6 per dollar of expected cost.

points.lead: Fewer defaults are a real gain:
points.text: a buyer facing one creditor, letters of credit and reform conditions defaults less often.

points.lead: The state bears risk cheaply only sometimes:
points.text: not when the utility and the treasury are in trouble together.

slides.title: Most of the expected cost falls on the buyers' owners, little on donors
slides.note: Liquidity, not loss, can break the facility: in a 1-in-200 year, 65% of buyers are in arrears together, so it needs a buffer of about $57m, a third of a year's $174m payments.
slides.source: Working paper 3.1, Table 4 and Proposition 3; correlation 0.3, six-month bridge (stylized).

slides.text: Letters of credit, a payment security fund and a central-bank debit of defaulting states protect the intermediary. The risk moved to the center; it was not removed.

slides.title: Design the facility so that the risk stays small

points.text: A dollar tariff hands the state the devaluation risk of every contract, in the crisis when it can least bear it.
7.7 cents falling to 3.9 by year 7 has the present value of a flat 5 cents, with 23% less owed after year 7.
Large markets build their own; small states share one, with a stronger multilateral layer.

points.lead: Reform as the price of entry,
points.text: and the guarantee recorded at expected cost under a published cap. Small versions already work: Zambia's IDA payment guarantee.

slides.source: Working paper 3.1, Sections 7–8; World Bank Group, Zambia Scaling Solar (2018).
